title: SELECT Basics
subtitle: Retrieve rows and columns from a table
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Data is stored in database tables. You need a way to retrieve specific rows and columns from those tables.
whyItExists.solution: The SELECT statement is the most fundamental SQL command. SELECT col1, col2 FROM table retrieves those columns from every row. Add WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT to narrow the results.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any time you want to read data from a database.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: SELECT doesn't modify data. For creating/changing data use INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.

explainModes.beginner: SELECT tells the database what columns you want. FROM tells it which table to look in. SELECT * means 'give me everything.' SELECT name, email means 'only these two columns.'
explainModes.simple: SELECT col1, col2 FROM table — basic retrieval. SELECT * FROM table — all columns. SELECT DISTINCT col FROM table — unique values only. SELECT col AS alias — rename column in output. LIMIT n — only return n rows. SELECT 1+1 — expressions without a table.
explainModes.standard: Column order in SELECT controls output order. Aliases (AS) are visible in ORDER BY but NOT in WHERE (use the expression again). DISTINCT removes duplicate rows across all selected columns. LIMIT / FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY (ANSI SQL) / TOP n (SQL Server). Calculated columns: SELECT price * 1.18 AS price_with_tax FROM products.
explainModes.technical: SELECT is evaluated conceptually in this order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. This explains why column aliases from SELECT cannot be used in WHERE. SELECT without FROM is valid in most databases (SQLite, PostgreSQL) — useful for expressions: SELECT 2+2, 'hello'. SQL keywords are case-insensitive; by convention write them uppercase.
explainModes.deepDive: The relational algebra operation for SELECT is projection (π) — choosing columns — and selection (σ) — filtering rows. DISTINCT is implemented as sort+dedup or hash-dedup by the engine — can be expensive. SELECT INTO (SQL Server) or CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (SQLite/PG) creates a new table from query results. In PostgreSQL, LATERAL joins allow correlated subqueries in FROM.

questions.question: What does SELECT * FROM products return?
options: Only the first row of products
All columns and all rows from the products table
An error — you must specify column names
questions.explanation: * is a wildcard meaning 'all columns.' SELECT * FROM products retrieves every column (id, name, category, price, stock) and every row in the products table.

faq.a: SQL keywords (SELECT, FROM, WHERE) are case-insensitive — SELECT, select, and Select are the same. Column and table names follow the database's rules — usually case-insensitive but best to match the exact case you created them with. String comparisons can be case-sensitive depending on the database's collation.

faq.q: What is the difference between AS and no alias?
faq.a: Without AS, the column in the output keeps its original name (or the expression text). With AS alias, the output column gets the alias name. Aliases make results more readable and are required for calculated columns. They're also how you reference aggregated columns in ORDER BY.

examples: SELECT user_id, SUM(total) AS lifetime_value FROM orders GROUP BY user_id
SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers — list all countries with customers
SELECT name, price * 1.18 AS price_incl_gst FROM products
